script.title: How a 1% fee can cost you $95,000

scenes.heading: A tiny fee?
scenes.narration: A fee of one percent a year sounds tiny. Over 30 years, it can cost you more than $95,000. Let's see how.
scenes.visual_brief:
#pergunta Can 1% cost you $95,000?
Open the loop.

scenes.heading: The example
scenes.narration: You invest $500 a month for 30 years. We assume 7% a year before fees, just to do the math. Real returns vary, and you can lose money.
scenes.visual_brief:
#lista $500 a month; 30 years; 7% a year before fees, assumed
Assumptions first.

scenes.heading: Two funds
scenes.narration: Fund A charges 0.1% a year. Fund B charges 1%. The fee comes out of your return every year, so A keeps 6.9% and B keeps 6%.
scenes.visual_brief:
#comparacao Fund A: 0.1% a year in fees; 6.9% left for you | Fund B: 1% a year in fees; 6% left for you
The only difference.

scenes.heading: Same money in
scenes.narration: Either way, you put in the same $180,000 over 30 years.
scenes.visual_brief:
#numero 180 | thousand dollars invested in both funds
Same effort.

scenes.heading: Thirty years later
scenes.narration: After 30 years, Fund A is worth about $598,000. Fund B, about $502,000.
scenes.visual_brief:
#grafico Value after 30 years, in thousands of dollars | Fund A=598; Fund B=502
The gap.

scenes.heading: The difference
scenes.narration: The difference is $95,827. That is more than half of everything you put in.
scenes.visual_brief:
#numero 95827 | dollars lost to a 0.9% higher fee
The price of 1%.

scenes.heading: Why so big
scenes.narration: The fee is charged on your whole balance, every year. As the balance grows, so does the fee, and the money taken by fees never compounds for you again.
scenes.visual_brief:
#causa The fee hits the whole balance => The balance grows => The fee grows with it
Fees compound too.

scenes.heading: The SEC says
scenes.narration: The SEC puts it this way: over time, even small ongoing fees have a big impact on your investment portfolio.
scenes.visual_brief:
#citacao Over time, even small ongoing fees have a big impact on your investment portfolio. | U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission
Official source.

scenes.heading: Where fees hide
scenes.narration: Where to look: the fund's expense ratio, any advisory fee, and account fees. Add them up to get your real yearly cost.
scenes.visual_brief:
#lista Fund expense ratio; Advisory fee; Account fees
What to check.

scenes.heading: Compare first
scenes.narration: Before you invest, find the total yearly fee and compare. A gap that looks smaller than one percent can become a six figure gap later. This is math, not investment advice.

sources.title: Investor Bulletin: How Fees and Expenses Affect Your Investment Portfolio

claims.text: $500 a month for 30 years at 6.9% (7% minus a 0.1% fee), compounded monthly, ends near $598,000 ($598,085). Calculo proprio.
The same at 6% (7% minus a 1% fee) ends near $502,000 ($502,258); the difference is $95,827. Calculo proprio.
Over time, even small ongoing fees have a big impact on your investment portfolio.
Ongoing fees include fund expenses, advisory fees and account fees.
